definition: Rude and ungracious in a petty, sulky way, especially when kindness or thanks is expected.
example: It would be churlish to complain about the rain when the farmers have waited months for it.
nuance: Churlish stresses a petty lack of grace or gratitude, while boorish stresses crude, clumsy manners.
prompt: A guest opens a handmade gift from the host at a holiday dinner.
options: Grumbling that the knitted scarf was itchy, Leo gave a churlish shrug instead of thanks.
The churlish guest hugged the host and praised every stitch of the green scarf.
Too young to read the card, the churlish toddler needed help opening the box.
Feeling churlish with joy, the guest wore the scarf for the rest of the night.
reasons: Meeting a kind gesture with sulky ingratitude is exactly this kind of petty rudeness.
Warm thanks and generous praise are the opposite of grudging rudeness.
The word does not mean childish; being small and needing help is not rude.
The word has a sour, unfriendly tone and cannot describe happiness or delight.

practice.prompt: A soccer team loses a close championship match to its rival.
options: The captain gave a churlish speech that generously credited the rivals for their skill.
After two overtime periods, the churlish players could barely lift their legs.
Calm and churlish, the coach reminded everyone that one loss would not define them.
Refusing to shake hands with the winners was a churlish end to an otherwise fine season.
reasons: Generously crediting opponents is gracious, not mean-spirited.
The word describes rudeness, not exhaustion; tired legs involve no bad manners.
A steady, encouraging message is kind, so it cannot be called ungracious.
Snubbing the victors out of spite shows a petty, graceless attitude.
